claims.text: Differences in atomic-size mismatch among the constituent elements produce variations in local lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortion governs mechanical-property differences by altering dislocation movement and twinning mechanisms.
The investigated quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys are single-phase FCC after standardized thermomechanical processing.
Removing one or more elements from equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni progressively reduces the overall lattice-distortion parameter.
Composition-dependent local lattice distortion produces changes in dislocation density, twinning, and stacking-fault formation.
Atomic-size mismatches generate local lattice strains.
Local lattice strains impede or otherwise modify dislocation motion.
Local lattice strains modify twin-boundary formation.
Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni has an optimal balance of lattice distortion and stacking-fault energy.
The balance of lattice distortion and stacking-fault energy in the quinary baseline produces synergistic strengthening and toughening.
Reduced-component alloys have diminished lattice distortion that alters slip and twinning behavior.
Alloys with fewer constituent elements have lower lattice distortion than equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
Alloys with fewer constituent elements will exhibit lower yield strengths than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Alloys with fewer constituent elements will exhibit modified ductility and reduced twinning activity relative to the quinary baseline.
Yield strength and ductility will correlate with measured reductions in local lattice strain across the composition series.
The proposed mechanism applies to single-phase FCC alloys within the Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni composition space under room-temperature deformation.
The mechanism may not apply to multiphase or non-FCC alloys or under substantially different temperatures or loading rates.
Dislocation theory and previous experimental correlations qualitatively support a role for lattice distortion.
